2.2.4.1-f10.accuracy_reason: Galen wrote a short treatise on exercise with the small ball (De parvae pilae exercitio).

2.2.4.1-f117.accuracy_reason: The quotation is accurate to Virgil, Eclogue 1.6–7, and the note correctly describes Burton's change to a plural relative clause while keeping the singular 'ille'.

2.2.4.1-f118.accuracy_reason: Aeneid 1.327 reads 'o quam te memorem, virgo?' (Aeneas to Venus). John Williams is the closest antecedent in Burton's sentence.

2.2.4.1-f123.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.1.34–35, goes on 'possis et magnam morbi deponere partem', as the note says.

2.2.4.1-f127.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.3–4, reads 'planius ac melius … dicit', and its subject is Homer. Burton's 'plenius' and 'dicunt' turn the line to the philosophers.

2.2.4.1-f133.accuracy_reason: These are Heron's Pneumatica (in Latin 'Spiritalia', translated by Commandino), Belopoeica and Automata.

2.2.4.1-f135.accuracy_reason: De superficierum divisionibus liber, attributed to Machometus Bagdedinus, was published at Pesaro in 1570 by Dee and Commandino.

2.2.4.1-f136.accuracy_reason: Commandino's Liber de centro gravitatis solidorum was published at Bologna in 1565.

2.2.4.1-f139.accuracy_reason: Bacon's Epistola de secretis operibus does say carriages may be made 'ut sine animali moveantur'.

2.2.4.1-f145.accuracy_reason: Fulminating gold is a correct description of an explosive gold compound known to seventeenth-century chemists.

2.2.4.1-f154.accuracy_reason: The weapon-salve was a Paracelsian sympathetic ointment applied to the weapon rather than the wound, as stated.

2.2.4.1-f158.accuracy_reason: Puteanus's Pietatis thaumata (1617) gave 1,022 permutations of Bauhusius's line to the Virgin.

2.2.4.1-f2.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epistles 1.2.27, reads 'fruges consumere nati'; Burton singularizes it.

2.2.4.1-f22.accuracy_reason: Tempe is the Peneus valley in Thessaly, and Burton's verse renders it as 'pleasant fields'.

2.2.4.1-f224.accuracy_reason: 'In fieri' is the scholastic phrase for 'in the process of being made', and Williams did found a library at Lincoln.

2.2.4.1-f261.accuracy_reason: The Field of the Cloth of Gold took place in June 1520, which correctly corrects the sidenote's 1519.

2.2.4.1-f263.accuracy_reason: Pro Archia 16 reads 'adulescentiam alunt, senectutem oblectant … delectant domi', so the reordering is described correctly.

2.2.4.1-f264.accuracy_reason: Odes 3.9 is indeed the amoebean dialogue with Lydia.

2.2.4.1-f267.accuracy_reason: Vulgate Psalm 118:140 reads 'ignitum eloquium tuum vehementer'.

2.2.4.1-f31.accuracy_reason: Lucan, Pharsalia 10, describes Cleopatra's banquet hall. The line goes on 'Tyrio quorum pars maxima fuco / cocta diu', so the coverlets are indeed dyed with Tyrian purple.

2.2.4.1-f310.accuracy_reason: Quercetanus is the Latin name of Joseph Du Chesne, who wrote the Diaeteticon polyhistoricon (1606).

2.2.4.1-f329.accuracy_reason: In the Vulgate, Proverbs 31:13 reads 'quaesivit lanam et linum' and 31:27 reads 'panem otiosa non comedit', so the note assigns each reference correctly.

2.2.4.1-f334.accuracy_reason: Burggravius's Biolychnium came with a tract on magnetic cure drawn from Paracelsus' Mumia. The two senses of mumia given (a drug from embalmed bodies, and the Paracelsian vital balsam) are both correct.

2.2.4.1-f337.accuracy_reason: The source (Velleius 2.107: an old German meets Tiberius on the Elbe) is right, and so is the point about Burton's error. But the claim that 'ullam' does not agree with a 'masculine' diem is shaky: dies is often feminine, so ullam can agree with it.

2.2.4.1-f38.accuracy_reason: The lines render Odyssey 4.71–75, and Burton's English 'Clear amber' confirms how he takes electrum.

2.2.4.1-f42.accuracy_reason: The lines render Iliad 22.159–161, on the chase around Troy, and Burton does say only 'the Poet'.

2.2.4.1-f49.accuracy_reason: Romolo Amaseo published a Latin translation of Pausanias, and Burton's sidenote names him.

2.2.4.1-f52.accuracy_reason: The quoted text of Georgics 1.139–140 is right, and 'insidias avibus moliri, incendere vepres' is Georgics 1.271.

2.2.4.1-f54.accuracy_reason: Saturn was the god of agriculture, and in 'Democritus to the Reader' Burton says Saturn was lord of his geniture (the planet ruling his birth).

2.2.4.1-f66.accuracy_reason: The lines are Juvenal 6.402–405, on the woman who gossips about everything, and the Seres are conventionally taken as the Chinese.

2.2.4.1-f69.accuracy_reason: Persius 5.57–58 reads 'hunc alea decoquit, ille / in Venerem putris', and 'decoquit' does mean to ruin or bankrupt.

2.2.4.1-f72.accuracy_reason: The note is right. Horace, Epistles 2.2.172–174, reads 'puncto mobilis horae / nunc prece, nunc pretio, nunc vi, nunc morte suprema / permutet dominos et cedat in altera iura'.

2.2.4.1-f78.accuracy_reason: The note implies Burton changed Augustine's verb, but Augustine himself writes 'melius enim utique tota die foderent, quam tota die saltarent' (Enarr. in Ps. 91.2). 'Arare' is only the common proverbial form, so Burton's 'fodere' may be faithful to Augustine.

2.2.4.1-f79.accuracy_reason: Cicero, Pro Murena 13, reads 'nemo enim fere saltat sobrius, nisi forte insanit'. Leaving out 'enim' does no harm.

2.2.4.1-f80.accuracy_reason: This is the standard definition of the fallacy ignoratio elenchi.

2.2.4.1-f83.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Histories 1.22, reads 'et vetabitur semper et retinebitur'.
